title: Lecture 5 – Parathyroid, calcium & bone

Source: CursV Parathyroid 2022.pptx – 54 slides

Parathyroid glands Topics: Hormones involved in the calcium metabolism regulation Hypercalcemia Hyperparathyroidism Hypocalcemia Hypoparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism Vitamin D deficiency Osteoporosis #1

Calcium #2

  • The bones contain approximately 99.5% of the total calcium in the body.
  • Calcium in the circulation
  • Circulating calcium exists in several forms (see Fig).
  • • Ionized—biologically active (50%).
  • • Complexed to citrate, phosphate, etc.—biologically active (5%).
  • • Bound to protein, mainly albumin—inactive (45%).

REGULATION OF CALCIUM METABOLISM Calcium-regulating hormones #3

  • Ionized Ca
  • [Ca 2+ ]
  • 2.2-2.7 mEq/l
  • Bone
  • Kidney
  • Intestinal mucosa
  • PTH
  • Calcitonin
  • PTH
  • 1,25(OH)2vitD3
  • (PTH)

1. PTH is an 84-amino-acid peptide #4

  • ← usually 4 parathyroid glands (located on the back of the
  • thyroid gland in variable locations) ±
  • - 1 or more may be ectopic, located throughout the neck or upper mediastinum, along the thymus descending line.
  • ectopic parathyroid glands →difficulties in localization
  • !!! the normal parathyroid gland weighs only about 40 mg
  • Biologic effects of PTH
  • PTH has several major actions, all serving to increase plasma calcium by:
  • on kidney – PTH has direct effects:  Ca reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubes,  reabsorption of Phosphate in the renal proximal tubule and of bicarbonate; additionally  the synthesis of 1,25(OH)2D3 in the proximal tubule by inducing transcription of the 1-hydroxylase gene
  • on intestinal mucosa : the effect of PTH on intestinal calcium absorption is indirect (a slow response), resulting from ↑ renal production of the intestinally active vit D metabolite1,25 (OH)2 D3
  • on bone: PTH ↑ both bone resorption (occurring rapidly) and bone formation ; with regard to calcium homeostasis, the effect of PTH on bone resorption is dominant!

2. Biologic effects of calcitonin #5

  • -is secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid
  • - On bone- inhibits osteoclastic-mediated bone resorbtion (= its principal function)
  • -on kidney: inhibits the reabsorption of phosphate and ↑ the renal excretion of calcium
  • Calcitonin (CT) is of clinical interest for two reasons.
  • First, CT is important as a tumor marker in MCT (medullary carcinoma of thyroid gland).
  • Second, CT has therapeutic uses as an inhibitor of osteoclastic bone resorption. CT can be administered either parenterally or as a nasal spray and is used in the treatment of Paget disease , hypercalcemia, and osteoporosis.

VitaminD3 is hydroxylated in #6

  • the liver →
  • to form 25-hydroxycholecalciferol→ [25(OH)D3]
  • (kidney)
  • 1α,25(OH)2D3(calcitriol)
  • PTH
  • 3. Vitamin D and its metabolites
  • 25 OH vitamin D (25OHD)
  • the main storage form of vitamin D
  • the most clinically useful measure of vitamin D status.
  • Levels over 50nmol/L are generally accepted as satisfactory and
  • Values <25nmol/L representing deficiency.
  • The major pathologic complication of vitamin D deficiency is rickets (in children) or osteomalacia (in adults)
  • Calcitriol (1,25 (OH)2D3), the active form of vitamin D, biologic effects:
  • -On the intestinal mucosa : (+) calcium and P reabsorption

REGULATION OF PARATHYROID HORMONE SECRETION PTH secretion is regulated by the serum Ca 2+ ( negative FB)→ ↓ Ca 2+ are detected by the calcium receptor of the parathyroid cells →↑ PTH secretion, while ↑ levels of Ca 2+→ ↓ PTH secretion #7

  • Ca++
  • (-)
  • Calcium sensing-receptor (CaSR)
  • PTH
  • -magneziu
  • -1,25(OH)2 vitamina D (-) PTH gene transcription
  • The extracellular calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), expressed on the parathyroid cell senses changes in extracellular calcium
  • Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism, characterized by alterations in the blood calcium levels and bone metabolism, are states of either surplus or deficient parathyroid function.

Hypercalcemia #8

  • In 5% of hospital patients and in 0.5% of the general population

Causes of hypercalcaemia #9

  • Confirm the diagnosis
  • Serum calcium/Ca2+ (several fasting serum calcium samples)
  • Determine the cause
  • Intact PTH (Ipth)
  • If the iPTH level is ↑, and thus inappropriate for hypercalcemia →parathyroid overactivity, primary hyperparathyroidism or rarely, tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
  • If the PTH is ↓→search for other entities (eg, malignancy)
  • Seek underlying illness
  • • History and examination.
  • • Chest X-ray, CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis (→ malignancy or granulomatous disease) FBC and ESR.
  • • 25OHD (rarely 1,25(OH)2D), parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) .
  • • Biochemical profile (renal and liver function); Thyroid function tests (exclude thyrotoxicosis).
  • • Plasma and urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation (exclude myeloma).
  • • Serum cortisol (short Synacthen® test (exclude Addison’s disease)).
  • Hyperparathyroidism is by far the most common cause of hypercalcemia.
  • Malignancy- associated hypercalcemia is the second most common form of hypercalcemia.
PTH-dependent hypercalcemia:   Hyperparathyroidism (primary, tertiary)     Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemiaPTH-independent hypercalcemia   Malignant disease Myeloma Secondary deposits in bone Production of osteoclastic factors by tumors PTH-related protein secretion Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases. Drugs: thiazide diuretics, lithium, vitD, vitA intoxication; vitD analogs Immobilization. Hyperthyroidism. Addison’s disease.

HYPERPARATHYROIDISM #10

Primary hyperparathyroidism is a hypercalcemic disorder that results from excessive, autonomic secretion of PTH. ETIOLOGY: Single parathyroid adenoma (80%) Parathyroid carcinoma-rare (1-2%) Primary hyperplasia of the parthyroids (15%) Primary hyperparathyroidism can occur as part of : MEN 1=parathyroid hyperplasia (primary hyperparathyroidism)+ pancreatic tumors+ pituitary tumors MEN 2a = medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MCT)+ pheochromocytoma+ parathyroid hyperplasia Hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome is a rare familial cause of hyperparathyroidism that may be associated with parathyroid carcinoma and maxillary or mandibular tumors. #11

Clinical features #12

  • The classic signs and symptoms of primary hyperparathyroidism:
  • renal disease-
  • classic hyperparathyroid bone disease –osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • = rarely seen nowadays
  • In fact, about 85% of patients are regarded as asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic.
  • 1.Bone disease
  • osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • Bone pain, and sometimes pathologic fracture
  • osteoporosis (preferential loss of cortical bone)
  • 2. Hyperparathyroid kidney disease
  • Kidney stones (they are usually calcium oxalate stones)(usually recurrent and severe)
  • Nephrocalcinosis (deposition of calcium in the renal medulla) ( clinically evident nephrocalcinosis rarely occurs, but a gradual loss of renal function is not uncommon)
  • Renal insufficiency [eGFR] <60 mL/min
  • polydipsia and polyuria← chronic hypercalcemia can also compromise the renal concentrating ability

A number of symptoms and signs accompany hypercalcemia: #13

  • • CNS effects: lethargy, depression, psychosis, ataxia, stupor, and coma;
  • • Neuromuscular effects: weakness, proximal myopathy, and hypertonia;
  • • Cardiovascular effects: hypertension, bradycardia (and eventually asystole), and a shortened QT interval
  • • Digestive effects: nausea, indigestion, vomiting, anorexia, constipation (sometimes even– ileus ← ↓bowel motility ←hypercalcemia), peptic ulcers, pancreatitis
  • • Eye findings such as band keratopathy;
  • • Systemic metastatic calcification: skin → itch; joints→ condrocalcinosis;

DIAGNOSIS OF primary hyperparathyroidism #14

  • B. Investigations aimed at determining the presence of end-organ damage from hypercalcaemia for clinical decision-making reasons.
  • C. Imaging-Localization studies of abnormal parathyroid glands
  • WORKUP
  • DIAGNOSTIC TESTS

DIAGNOSIS OF primary hyperparathyroidism #15

  • Laboratory findings (calcium and phosphorus metabolism)
  • Ionized calcium or total calcium=↑
  • Serum phosphorus is low-normal or ↓ (< 3,5 mg/dl)
  • Urinary calcium=↑ (this should be measured in a young patient with modest elevation in calcium and PTH to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia)
  • Urinary phosphorus=↑
  • ↑ of AP level –reflecting high bone turnover (in severe parathyroid bone disease)
  • Renal function. This is usually normal but should be measured as a baseline.
  • Hormonal determinations
  • Intact PTH level=↑ ( an elevated level of PTH is clearly inappropriate in a hypercalcemic patient and establishes the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism); in a patient with ↑ PTH level, there is no need to screen for metastatic malignancy, sarcoidosis etc
  • Other: 1,25(OH)2D3 = ↑
  • .
  • The diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is merely biochemical and consists of ↑Ca +↑iPTH

Slide 16 #16

  • B. Investigations aimed at determining the presence of end-organ damage from hypercalcaemia for clinical decision-making reasons.

bone cysts or #17

  • brown tumors-
  • evident as osteolytic lesion
  • Subperiosteal resorption, the most sensitive and specific radiologic finding of osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • -X-rays: of the phalanges – classic subperiosteal resorption of cortical bone of phalanges
  • -skull X-ray: a similar process leads to a “salt and paper” appearance
  • Bone cysts, usually multiple, which contain a brownish serous fluid: in the central medullary portions of the shafts of the metacarpals, ribs or pelvis.
  • Osteoclastomas or “ brown trumors “, composed of osteoclasts admixed with stromal cells and matrix; are found most often in trabecular portions of the jaw, the long bones and ribs.
  • Pathologic fractures
  • Dental films may disclose loss of the lamina dura of the teeth
  • B. X-rays are often obtained to determine whether operative intervention is indicated.
  • Skeletal radiographs (lateral thoracolumbar spine, hands and skull, ribs, femur etc) - radiographic features include:

Plain x-ray →nephrocalcinosis, renal stones #18

  • Renal tract ultrasound (calculi, nephrocalcinosis).
  • B. + renal function (U&E) and renal imaging (abdominal radiograph, ultrasound, CT scan for renal stones) are often obtained to determine whether operative intervention is indicated.

Bone mineral density by DXA (dual X-ray absorptiometry) →osteoporosis #19

  • B.+determinations of BMD are often obtained to determine whether operative intervention is indicated.

C.Localization studies of abnormal parathyroid glands This should only form part of a preoperative assessment and is not indicated in the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism (!!!the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is merely biochemical: ↑Ca +↑PTH). The most successful procedures are 99mTc-sestamibi scanning +SPECT/CT, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and ultrasound. Individually, each has a sensitivity of 60% to 80% Used in combination → 80% ! Are essential in in the management of patients with recurrent or persistent hyperparathyroidism #20

The definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism= parathyroidectomy. #21

  • Many patients =asymptomatic or at most minimally symptomatic → ??? questions about the role of parathyroid surgery in primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Indications for surgery in primary hyperparathyroidism
  • It is generally accepted that all patients with symptomatic hyperparathyroidism or evidence of end-organ damage should be considered for parathyroidectomy.
  • This would include:
  • • Definite symptoms of hypercalcaemia.
  • • Impaired renal function (eGFR< 60ml/min).
  • • Renal stones (symptomatic or on radiograph).
  • • Parathyroid bone disease, especially osteitis fibrosis cystica; BMD DXA T-score <-2.5 SD; vertebral fractures
  • • Pancreatitis.
  • Significant hypercalciuria
  • Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of the reference range.
  • MANAGEMENT

Surgery in primary hyperparathyroidism/parathyroidectomy. 2 options: minimally invasive surgery bilateral neck exploration if localizing studies (with two separate techniques (usually US and 99mTc-sestamibi)) clearly indicate a single abnormal gland and if introperative PTH testing is available ► surgical management generally consists of unilateral exploration (minimally invasive surgery) of the neck with the removal of the single abnormal gland. ►otherwise – a bilateral neck exploration by an experienced surgeon is optimal in the first instance- in which all 4 glands are identified and all enlarged glands removed is preferred. In patients with hyperplasia, the preferred operation is partial parathyroidectomy (3 ½ -gland parathyroidectomy), leaving a remnant sufficient to prevent hypocalcemia (perhaps with reimplantation of tissue in more accessible site). #22

After a successful parathyroidectomy a transitory postoperative hypocalcemia may appear: ← functional inhibition of the remnant parathyroid glands ←” hungry bone syndrome” ← avid uptake of calcium and phosphate by the bones treated with calcium + active vitamin D metabolites #23

Conservative management #24

  • There is no definitive medical therapy for primary hyperparathyroidism
  • -calcium restriction
  • -bisphosphonates (Alendronat etc), Selective estrogen response modulator SERM (raloxifen®)
  • -Calcimimetic agents
  • (FDA-approved for the management of secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients with CKD on dialysis and of primary hyperparathyroidism as well in US))
  • that activate the parathyroid CaSR, may offer an alternative to surgery (for controlling hyperCa):
  • for individuals who meet guidelines for surgical referral but who are too sick or unwilling to undergo surgery or in whom surgery has failed to cure their hyper PTH
  • Cinacalcet® ( to ↓/normalize serum [Ca2+] and raise serum phosphate with modest lowering of PTH levels in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism)

SECONDARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM #25

  • PTH=↑ as appropriate for a ↓ Ca 2+
  • Causes:
  • Chronic renal failure
  • Vit D deficit
  • CLINIC
  • OSTEITIS FIBROSA
  • OSTEOMALACIA
  • LABORATORY
  • Ca/n, PTH, 25 oh-vitamin D 
  • TREATMENT : Calcitriol or vitamin D analog, calcium supplementation, phosphate restriction
  • TERTIARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM –occurs after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism, if 1 or more glands act autonomously (eg with adenoma formation)

HYPOCALCEMIA #26

Slide 27 #27

  • HYPOCALCEMIA ►normal serum Calcium ←PTH and ←1,25(OH)2D =central to the defense against hypocalcemia
  • → hypocalcemic disorders and chronic hypocalcemia can result from :
  • a failure to secrete PTH,
  • altered responsiveness to PTH,
  • a deficiency of vitamin D, or
  • a resistance to vitamin D.

Causes of Hypocalcemia #28

  • Chronic hypocalcemia
  • a.Hypoparathyroidism
  • b. Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP)
  • isolated resistance to PTH, which presents with the biochemical features of hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • PHP type IA and PHP type IB
  • c. Failure to produce 1,25(OH)2D normally
  • Severe Vitamin D deficiency
  • Hereditary vitamin D-dependent rickets, type 1 (renal 25-OH-vitamin D 1alpha-hydroxylase deficiency,inactivating CYP27B1 mutations)
  • d. Resistance to 1,25(OH)2D action
  • Hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, type 2 (defective Vit D Receptor)
  • Acute hypocalcemia
  • - is most often the consequence of an overwhelming challenge to the adaptive response such as rhabdomyolysis, in which a flood of phosphate from injured skeletal muscle inundates the extracellular fluid
  • ←acute complexation or deposition of calcium
  • Acute hyperphosphatemia (←rhabdomyolysis, rapid tumor lysis)
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Rapid, excessive skeletal mineralization
  • Hungry bones syndrome
  • Osteoblastic metastasis

Clinical features #29

  • A.The clinical features of hypocalcaemia are largely as a result of ↑neuromuscular excitability.
  • In order of ↑ severity, these include:
  • • Tingling—especially of fingers, toes, or lips.
  • • Numbness—especially of fingers, toes, or lips.
  • • Cramps.
  • • Carpopedal spasm= the classic muscular component of tetany
  • Tetany crisis is the hallmark of severe hypocalcemia
  • Tetany can involve other muscle groups, including life-threatening spasm of laryngeal muscles
  • • Stridor due to laryngospasm.
  • •Focal or generalized seizures; confusion
  • Lesser degrees of neuromuscular excitability produce latent tetany which can be elicited by testing for:
  •  Chvostek sign:
  •  Trousseau sign:

Other manifestations of hypocalcemia #30

  • -hyperirritability, anxiety and depression, shortness of breath
  • -cardiac effects: prolongation of QT intervals; excitation-contraction coupling may be impaired, and refractory congestive heart failure is sometimes observed, particularly in patients with underlying cardiac disease.
  • -ophtalmologic effects: subcapsular cataract
  • -dermatologic effects: dry skin, coarse hair, brittle nails
  • -In children: dental and enamel hypoplasia (if hypocalcaemia is present during the development of permanent teeth).
  • 20% of children with chronic hypocalcemia develop mental retardation.

Slide 31 #31

  • In addition, there may be clinical signs and symptoms associated with the underlying condition:
  • • Vitamin D deficiency may be associated with lethargy, generalized bone pain, fractures, or proximal myopathy
  • • Hypoparathyroidism can be accompanied by mental slowing and personality disturbances as well as extrapyramidal signs due to calcifications of basal ganglia (development of a parkinsonism-like syndrome), cataracts, and papilloedema (see also later)

Slide 32 #32

  • It is an endocrine disease with low calcium and inappropriately low (insufficient) circulating PTH levels.
  • Hypoparathyroidism (hypoPT) is the only major endocrine condition today, where the hormonal insufficiency in general is not treated by substitution of the missing hormone (PTH).
  • HYPOPARATHYROIDISM

Hypoparathyroidism #33

Etiology:
Postsurgical (← cancer surgery, total thyroidectomy and parathyroidectomy)
Autoimmune ( in the setting of type I polyglandular autoimmune syndrome (mutation in the autoimmune regulator of endocrine function (AIRE) gene): may be associated with primary adrenal insufficiency and mucocutaneous candidias)/ or as an isolated finding (with autoantibodies to the CaSR)
Other rare genetic conditions that can cause HypoPT either as part of a syndrome (e.g. DiGeorge syndrome= congenital absence of of the parathyroids and thymus: with thymic aplasia, immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies ) or as an isolated endocrinopathy
Infiltration ( hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease…)
Postirradiation (radioactive radioiodine therapy for Graves’ disease)
Idiopathic

Slide 34 #34

  • Clinical features (in addition to those common to all forms of hypocalcemia, presented above)
  • Complications and renal implications of chronic HypoPTH
  • Patients with chronic HypoPT seem to have lower QoL, muscle complaints, including fatigue and weakness, more anxiety and tendency to depression
  • HypoPT has traditionally been associated with
  • calcium-containing urolithiasis (the hypocalciuric effect of PTH has been lost) and
  • renal impairment (chronic renal insufficiency)
  • ← an ↑calcium–phosphate product.

Laboratory findings: Hypoparathyroidism Hypocalcemia (↓ total calcium,↓ionized calcium) Hypercalciuria Hyperphosphatemia ( because the phosphaturic effect of PTH is lost) Urinary phosphate ↓ Low or undetectable PTH level Serum and urine creatinine (these test for renal disease) ECG ; prolongation of QT interval Electromyographically, tetany is typified by repetitive motor neuron action potentials, usually grouped as doublets. #35

Treatment of hypocalcaemia #36

  • • Acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia is a medical emergency and demands urgent treatment whatever the cause.
  • • Treatment of chronic hypocalcaemia is more dependent on the cause.

HYPOPARATHYROIDISM TREATMENT Objectives: the patient should be free of symptoms or signs of hypocalcemia and the target serum calcium should be at the low end of the reference range. Standard treatment includes oral calcium salts and active vitamin D metabolites: Calcium supliments, orally - 1-3 g of elemental calcium /day in divided doses (500 mg/dose) Activated vitamin D metabolites: 1-calcidol (ALPHA-D3) [Alfacalcidiol is rapidly activated in the liver to 1,25(OH)2D] : 1-4 g/day 1,25(OH)2vitD3 ( calcitriol) (ROCALTROL)-1-3 g/day An adequate vitamin D status: vitamin D supplementations in a daily dose of 400–800 IU Magnesium PTH (1-84) - may improve quality of life. MANAGEMENT OF acute hypocalcaemia (TETANY CRISIS) Patients with tetany or seizures require urgent IV treatment with calcium gluconate. Calcium gluconate 10% (1f= 10 ml of calcium gluconate -93 mg of elemental calcium) by slow iv infusion, 1-2 amp. Diazepam, anxiolytics rebreathing into a paper bag oral calcium and a rapidly acting preparation of vit D (eg., calcitriol) should be started #37

VIT D deficiency #38

  • ←Results from one or more factors:
  • inadequate sunlight exposure,
  • inadequate nutrition,
  • malabsobtion
  • Clinical features
  • Lethargy, generalized bone pain, fractures, or proximal myopathy
  • Laboratory
  • Low-normal/ Hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, low urine calcium
  • ↑iPTH
  • A low serum 25 (OH) D level is diagnostic
  • Treatment is best given in the form of calciferol to restore body stores, correct biochemical abnormalities, and heal bony abnormalities.
  • Replacement doses of vitD: 800-2000 UI/day
  • Vigantoletten® 500-1000 UI
  • Vigantol ®drop(1 drop ≈ 600 UI): 2-6 drops/day
  • Daily intake of CALCIUM: approximately 1000-1200 mg/day

Pseudohypoparathyroidism #39

  • =is a heritable disorder of target-organ unresponsiveness to PTH
  • ←most commonly caused by autosomal dominant mutation of GNAS gene.
  • PHP type IB = isolated resistance to PTH, which presents with the biochemical features of hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism

PHP type IA #40

  • has, in addition to these biochemical features, a characteristic somatic phenotype known as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO):
  • -short stature, round face, short neck, obesity, brachydactyly (short digits), shortened metatarsals and metacarpals, subcutaneous ossifications, and often reduced intelligence.
  • Also TSH, LH, FSH, and GH signaling can be affected

Biochemical: #41

  • Hypocalcemia
  • Hyperphosphatemia
  • ↑ iPTH and there is a markedly blunted response to the administration of PTH
  • Treatment : the same like in hypoparathyroidism

Osteoporosis #42

  • Metabolic bone disease
  • reduction in the amount of bony tissue within the skeleton (low bone mass)
  • loss of structural integrity of the internal architecture of the bone
  • ►to enhanced bone fragility and an ↑ in fracture risk.
  • osteoporotic bone is at high risk of fracture, even after trivial injury

Slide 43 #43

  • The most common osteoporotic fractures are those of the hip, wrist (Colles’), and compression fractures of vertebral bodies.
  • !!!!Any fracture, other than those affecting fingers, toes, or face, which is caused by a fall from standing height or less is called a fragility (low-trauma) fracture, and underlying osteoporosis should be considered.

Underlying causes of osteoporosis #44

  • I. Primary Osteoporosis
  • =reduced bone mass and fractures in postmenopausal women (postmenopausal osteoporosis) or in older men and women due to age-related factors.
  • II. Secondary Osteoporosis (= bone loss resulting from specific clinical disorders or drugs etc)
  • 1.Endocrine disorders
  • Hypogonadism
  • Hyperprolactinemia
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Hyperthyroidism
  • GH deficiency or IGF-1 deficiency
  • Insulin dependent diabetes mellitus
  • 2. Gastrointestinal /nutrition disorders
  • Malabsorption syndromes: celiac disease, intestinal by-pass, chronic pancreatitis
  • Obstructive jaundice, billiary cirrhosis
  • 3. Hematologic disorders:
  • Multiple myeloma, systemic mastocytosis,leukemia
  • 4. Inflammatory conditions:
  • Rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • 5. Collagen metabolism disorders
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta
  • 6. Medications: GnRH agonists, cyclosporine, systemic glucocorticoids

Presentation of osteoporosis #45

  • • Usually clinically silent until an acute fracture.
  • Typical vertebral fracture:
  • Sudden episode of well-localized pain.
  • Pain may initially require bed rest but gradually subsides over 4–8 weeks; even after this time, there may be residual pain at the fracture site.
  • Following vertebral fracture, a patient may be left with persistent back pain, kyphosis, or height loss.
  • Peripheral fractures after lowtrauma are also more common in osteoporosis.
  • Osteoporosis does not cause generalized skeletal pain!!.

Osteoporosis Workup #46

  • 1 Establish the diagnosis
  • 2 Elucidate the cause and the differential diagnosis
  • The diagnosis of osteoporosis may be obvious in patients who have sustained fragility fractures
  •  the challenge →high-risk patients who have not yet sustained a fracture
  • Bone Densitometry- DXA
  • BMD is a highly significant predictor of fracture risk  noninvasive methods to estimate BMD are required to identify high-risk patients
  • Measurement of BMD with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)= the gold standard for the diagnosis of osteoporosis→ offers the most precise measurement for the least amount of radiation exposure.

DXA #47

  • Measures areal BMD (mineral per surface area rather than a true volumetric density), usually of the lumbar spine and proximal femur (hip) (± radius).
  • Gives BMD in g/cm2, which is difficult to interpret so→ translated to T or Z score
  • T-score: generated by comparing result with female, white, aged 20–29 years taken from the NHANES III study database.
  • Z score: generated by comparing result with person of same age, sex and ethnicity (describes the number of SDs by which the BMD in an individual differs from the mean value expected for age and sex ) ( used to suggest further evaluation)

Slide 48 #48

  • Site-specific measurement BMD:Femoral neck BMD, total hip BMD and total posteroanterior lumbar spine BMD
  • WHO defines osteoporosis as a bone density of 2.5 standard SDs below the young healthy adult mean value (T-score ≤−2.5) or lower.
  • However, this definition should not be applied to younger populations.
  • Z scores ≤−2.0 is ‘low BMD for age’
  • Interpretation of Z scores is complex
  • It is used to report BMD in pre-menopausal women and men aged <50, in children and adolescents.;
  • → suggests that additional tests may be required (? secondary osteoporosis)
  • Interpretation of DXA

2. Lateral thoracic and lumbar spine X-rays #49

  • are useful for detecting vertebral fractures including previously
  • asymptomatic vertebral fractures and for their follow-up
  • 3. Fracture risk assessment:
  • Use of fracture risk algorithms is now available to determine
  • individuals’ fracture risk (e.g. http://www.shef.ac.uk/FRAX).
  • -even though low BMD is strongly associated with the risk of fracture, it is well recognized that different risk factors, such as age, history of a prior fragility fracture, steroid use, and many others, are independent contributors to the risk of fracture and improve the sensitivity of BMD measurement in identifying patients at high risk of fracture
  • FRAX is a diagnostic tool that integrates:
  • clinical risk factors and
  • bone mineral density at the femoral neck
  • to calculate the 10-year probability of hip fracture and the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture.
  • Such an approach can help tune therapies to those patients at heightened risk of fracture
  • →treatment is generally indicated if a 10-year major fracture risk ≥20% or hip fracture risk ≥ 3%

Slide 50 #50

  • 4. Laboratory studies (employed to exclude secondary osteoporosis)- to establish the cause and for differential diagnosis
  • Erytrocytes sedimentation rate (ESR),
  • complete blood count (CBC),
  • ALT, AST, urea and creatinine levels,
  • serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase
  • TSH, FT4±
  • parathyroid hormone (PTH), urinary free cortisol level,
  • Testosterone and gonadotropin levels (FSH, LH),
  • ±25(OH) vitamin D,
  • serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP),
  • anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (if any suggestion of coeliac disease) etc
  • It is helpful to target these investigations at those people who have a significantly lower than expected bone mass for their age (Z score <–2).

Treatment #51

  • Therapeutic goals
  • ↓ risk for fractures
  • ↑ bone mineral density
  • Life style measures:
  • Encourage weight-bearing exercise (eg, leg-strengthening exercises), Encourage well-balanced diet
  • Falls prevention and hip protectors
  • Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake: optimal intake of calcium: ≈ 1000-1200 mg/day; vitamin D supplementation should be added (800-1000 UI/day in menopause); proteins

Pharmacologic Agents: #52

  • !!! NB. If vertebral fragility fracture (or other types of fragility fracture) is identified, treatment for osteoporosis is indicated irrespective of T-score
  • Antiresorptive:
  •  Bisphosphonates
  •  Calcitonin
  •  SERM (Selective estrogen receptor modulators)
  •  Hormone replacement therapy (estrogen)
  •  Denosumab (monoclonal antibody directed against RANKL): Prolia® 60 mg every 6 months sc
  • Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Risendronate, Zoledronic acid)
  • • Weekly (PO), monthly (PO), 3-monthly (IV), and annual (IV) preparations are available.
  • Oral bisphosphonates should be taken on an empty stomach, and 30–60min (dependent on drug) should pass prior to additional oral intake.
  • Side effects: GI disturbance, including nausea and oesophagitis, are common; osteonecrosis of the jaw is a very rare side effect;
  • -there is a possible association between atypical subtrochanteric femoral fractures in patients who have taken several years of bisphosphonates.
  • B. Osteo-anabolic (bone-forming) agents:
  •  Recombinant human PTH (1-34) (Teriparatide): given in daily subcutaneous doses: 20µg (for 2 years)

Take home messages!!!! #53

  • In the setting of hypercalcemia: first step=check PTH!
  • ↑Ca +↑ PTH= primary hyperparathyroidism
  • a fragility (low-trauma) fracture →underlying osteoporosis should be considered.
  • Osteoporosis does not cause generalized skeletal pain.
